newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CBA PROFIT FORECASTS LOWERED SLIGHTLY.
newsitem.headline: CBA PROFIT FORECASTS LOWERED SLIGHTLY.

text.p: Vicious pressure on home loan margins and little prospect of cost cuts are expected keep Commonwealth Bank of Australia's (CBA) annual profit in 1997/98 flat or even push it down slightly, analysts said on Wednesday.

They said CBA's result for the year to June 30, announced earlier, was within expectations but the strong margin pressure evident in the result and the bank's bearish comments may push some forcasts slightly lower.
Profit upgrades were unlikely, the analysts said.

CBA's pre-abnormal profit rose eight percent to A$1.206 billion, well within expectations of a profit of A$1.114 billion to A$1.240 billion. Net profit after abnormals fell four percent to A$1.078 billion after an abnormal post-tax loss of A$128 million for a planned technology restructuring.
CBA also announced a widely-expected A$650 million share buy-back to return excess capital.
"The result was marginally disappointing," said ANB AMRO Hoare Govett banking analyst Michael Pulman, who had forecast at the higher end of expectations.
Analysts said they now expected CBA to post about A$1.18 billion to A$1.2 billion in 1997/98, down from the average A$1.23 billion forecast by analysts in BZW's Barcep survey before the result.
Pulman pointed to weaker than expected net interest income because of margin pressure for a lower than expected second half result.
He said he had been forecasting a 1997/98 net profit of about A$1.18 billion before the result and this was unlikely to change much.
First Pacific Stockbroking banking analyst Andrew Turner said a profit forecast range of about A$1.18 billion to A$1.2 billion was now fair.

Slimmer margins and extra costs of about A$20 million to A$30 million from the share buyback were expected to ebb away at the bottom line, he said. "I wouldn't think they'd get over A$1,200 million now," Turner said.
Earnings per share forecasts were likely to be improve, however, because of the share buy-back, analysts said.
The higher than generally expected final dividend of 57 cents per share, up from 52 cents a year earlier, had also heartened investors, they said.
Some analysts said they remained concerned about CBA's inability to significantly reduce costs in the year and the size of the drop in the margin.

The results included an increase in CBA's cost to income ratio in the second half to 62 percent from 60 percent in the first half and CBA's group net interest margin fell to 3.41 percent from four percent over the year.
Over the last year CBA has led the major banks in a price war against non-banks funded by securitisation.
CBA has carved 120 basis points from its home loan margin and spent extra to promote its new products and increase its market share to 22.4 percent from 21.6 percent a year earlier.
Analysts said CBA appeared not have ended its sometimes expensive campaign to regain market share lost to the non-banks in the last three to four years.
First Pacific's Turner said Murray had told analysts the bank wanted to reclaim its market share.
"The use of the word reclaim scared me a bit," he said.
"I think they're in an environment where given their balance sheet structure and the risk on their interest margins, they should be far more aggressive on costs," he said.
Murray's comments at a news conference about rising unit labour costs and over A$100 million in costs to cure the Year 2000 millenium bug were not reassuring, analysts said.

CBA's stock was not expected to suffer much because of the results as the share buy-back and the strong dividend were likely to soothe away most concerns, they said. CBA shares closed down nine cents at A$16.28 in a weak market overall.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
